title: Proportional Symbols & Flow Lines

problems_fixed.what: Display gave no numeric route to the stored answer: it said only that Glasgow and Edinburgh had similar-sized circles, so no student could reach 636 thousand. Stored solution left untouched; the display now supplies the two ruler measurements the map actually encodes. Verified by pixel-measuring the real map: key 500 circle radius 10.42 px, Glasgow 11.79 px, ratio 1.131, so 500 x 1.131 squared = 640, i.e. Glasgow's true 635,640. Measurements given as 25.0 mm and 28.2 mm reproduce the stored answer exactly ((28.2/25.0)^2 x 500 = 636.2).
problems_fixed.old: The key shows that a circle representing 2,000,000 people has roughly twice the diameter of one representing 500,000 people. Glasgow and Edinburgh have similar-sized circles. Using the key, estimate Glasgow's population in thousands.
problems_fixed.new: The key shows that a circle representing 2,000,000 people has roughly twice the diameter of one representing 500,000 people, because the area of the circle carries the value. On a printed copy the 500 key circle measures 25.0 mm across and Glasgow's circle measures 28.2 mm across. Estimate Glasgow's population in thousands, to the nearest thousand.

misconceptions_note: All 20 original misconceptions used check:'wrong' (fired on any wrong answer) and 20 of 20 stated the correct answer outright, e.g. bronze[1] 'comes from Birmingham (60,000)' and silver[0] 'approximately 636,000'. All deleted. Replaced with 43 expect-matched errors (2 per problem, 3 where a third determinate error exists), every one derived by actually committing the error. Numeric expects verified: silver[0] linear scaling 564, wrong key circle 2545, people-not-thousands 636000; silver[1] 30000 and 120; silver[3] 65000, -25000, 25; gold[0] 135000, 105, 45. Multiple-choice expects are distractor indices.
flagged_unverifiable: flow-line-uk.png: the key heading reads 'Migration (thousands/yr)' but the three reference labels read 15,000 / 30,000 / 60,000, so the heading and the numbers disagree by a factor of a thousand. The image is a preserved stimulus so it has not been touched, and all walks read the labels at face value (60 = sixty thousand a year), matching every stored solution. Worth regenerating the image at some point.

proportional-symbol-uk.png: city labels are drawn offset from their circles (Glasgow's label sits left of its circle, Manchester's overlaps Leeds'). Nothing stored is wrong, but bronze[0] and silver[4] rely on the reader pairing label to circle, so a misconception was added for exactly that slip.
opener_concept: Two towns drawn as circles (Barton's twice the width of Ashby's) with a thin arrow into one and an arrow three times as thick into the other, all shown as inline SVG. Box 1 asks which town has more people, answerable by pure common sense from the picture. Box 2 says 5,000 people moved into Ashby and the Barton arrow is 3 times as thick, so how many moved into Barton (15,000), again common sense. The reveal then names both moves: a proportional symbol carries its value in the size of the shape, a flow line carries it in the thickness of the arrow with the arrowhead giving direction, and flags that circles scale by area rather than width, which is the silver rung.
notes: Both stimulus images were fetched from R2 and read directly, then pixel-measured (connected-component radii on the symbol map, distance-transform widths on the flow map), so nothing was guessed. Symbol map is genuinely area-proportional: key circles measure r = 10.42 / 21.26 / 43.84 px for 500 / 2,000 / 8,000 thousand. Measured city radii recover London ~9,700, Birmingham ~1,180, Glasgow ~640, Sheffield ~557, Manchester ~547, Liverpool ~498, Bristol ~467, Cardiff ~362, Belfast ~343, Newcastle ~283, Plymouth ~264, Aberdeen and Norwich ~200 thousand, all matching real populations, so every stored answer in the bank is correct as it stands. Flow map: key line widths 4.0 / 6.0 / 10.0 px for 15 / 30 / 60 thousand; the Birmingham arrow measures 10.0 (widest into London), Manchester 7.2, Leeds 4.5, confirming bronze[1], bronze[6] and silver[1] as stored. Three blue arrowheads land on London and two red arrows leave it, confirmed by crop inspection. No stored answer was changed anywhere. All 16 image references and both image URLs preserved byte-for-byte; no URL invented. Added: bronze/silver/gold_description (geography had none), tier_guides for all three tiers, guided.opener, guided.teach for all three tiers (each on its own self-contained inline SVG rather than a reused map, so every taught value is one I control and can verify), guided_steps on all 20 problems including all 16 multiple-choice ones (none needed guided_skip_reason: every one is reachable by counting on the stimulus or by classifying the options, so none is purely evaluative), and a plain-text hint on every problem. Every map or chart walk opens by locating on the stimulus: find the key box, count the arrowheads at London, find Glasgow in central Scotland, count the circles in the northern cluster. Completion boundaries put locating and key-reading in the pre-worked half and leave the reading-through, the calculation and the check live, at least two boxes each. Every walk ends on a check box with a done note explaining why the check proves the answer. related_videos, topic_links, image, options, calculator and solutions all preserved unchanged.
